fieldtest.title: A $2 Test Turned Blue. She Served 21 Days. Police Still Carry the Kits.
fieldtest.description:
In August 2010, in a strip-mall parking lot in Houston, a police officer dropped a small white crumb from Amy Albritton's car floor into a vial of pink liquid. If it stayed pink, everyone could go home. It turned blue. She was not driving — she was the passenger in her own car. Nine hours later she was booked into the Harris County jail.

The kit cost about $2 and had changed little since 1973. On the evidence submission form the officer wrote ".02 grms crack cocaine." Inside two days, with a court-appointed lawyer and an offer of 45 days instead of a two-year felony maximum, she pleaded guilty. She served 21 days.

On 23 February 2011 — roughly six months later — an analyst at the Houston Police Department crime laboratory put the evidence through a gas chromatograph-mass spectrometer. The remainder weighed 0.0134 grams, about the same, she noted, as a tiny pinch of salt. It matched nothing in the laboratory's database. It was not a drug. The examination sheet recorded "N.C.S. No controlled substance identified." Laboratories rarely notify officers when a false positive comes back, so nothing happened. Albritton had already lost her job, and the job was her apartment.

She was not alone. Reviewing its own files, the Harris County District Attorney's office found 416 uncorrected "variants" between January 2004 and June 2015, every one of them ending in a guilty plea; in 251 the laboratory result was simply "No Controlled Substance." Of 301 that began as Houston Police arrests, 212 rested on evidence the laboratory determined was not a controlled substance. All 212 pleaded guilty; 93 percent were sentenced to jail or prison; 50 had no prior drug conviction. Fifty-nine percent of the wrongfully convicted were Black, in a city whose Black population is 24 percent. The office that won those convictions is the office that found them: 119 struck from the record by the summer of 2016, more than 250 overturned in Houston by 2020.

The warnings were older than the cases. The National Bureau of Standards said in 1974 that the kits "should not be used as sole evidence for the identification of a narcotic or drug of abuse." By 1978 the Department of Justice had determined they "should not be used for evidential purposes." The chemical involved, cobalt thiocyanate, turns blue for cocaine and for more than 80 other compounds, "including methadone, certain acne medications and several common household cleaners." The results are inadmissible at trial in nearly every jurisdiction — but in Harris County in this period, 99.5 percent of felony convictions arrived by plea. Charles McClelland, who commanded the Houston Police Department, put it plainly: "Police officers aren't chemists. We shouldn't be doing field tests on the hood of patrol cars."

What followed was narrower than it sounds. Texas House Bill 34 did not require laboratory confirmation; it ordered a study. Houston stopped using the kits in July 2017, and the stated rationale was officer safety from fentanyl exposure, not accuracy. A 2024 study by the Quattrone Center for the Fair Administration of Justice found that roughly 773,000 drug arrests a year in the United States involve colour-based field tests, that roughly 30,000 a year involve people who do not possess illegal substances, and that Black Americans experience these erroneous arrests at about three times the rate of white Americans. In March 2026 Colorado enacted House Bill 26-1020, passed 65-0 and 33-0 and signed on 26 March, barring arrest for misdemeanour drug possession where a colour-change field test is the sole basis; reporting on the bill describes it as the first state law in the country to do so.

Albritton's conviction was later set aside. Asked whether that ended it, she said: "No. You're not ever free and clear of it. It follows you everywhere you go."

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic, and no real-person likeness is shown.

Sources include: ProPublica and The New York Times Magazine reporting by Ryan Gabrielson and Topher Sanders; the Houston Police Department crime laboratory examination record as quoted in that reporting; the Harris County District Attorney's office and its conviction integrity unit; the National Bureau of Standards; the United States Department of Justice; the Timothy Cole Exoneration Review Commission; Texas House Bill 34; the Quattrone Center for the Fair Administration of Justice at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School; and Colorado House Bill 26-1020 and the Colorado General Assembly's legislative record.

#FieldDrugTest #WrongfulConviction #CriminalJustice #ForensicScience #PleaBargain #PrimeDocumentary

lejeune.title: He Buried His Daughter at Nine. 408,000 Have Filed. One Claim Paid $405.
lejeune.description:
In September 1985 a Marine Corps drill instructor named Jerry Ensminger lost his nine-year-old daughter, Janey, to leukemia. She was ill for nearly two and a half years. The family was told what families are always told — that these things happen, and nobody is at fault. Ensminger had given the Corps twenty-four and a half years, and he believed them. He and his wife had lived in base family housing at Tarawa Terrace from 1973 to 1975, and she spent the first three months of her pregnancy there.

The base measured its own water and wrote down what it found. In October 1980 an Army Environmental Hygiene Agency team ran routine trihalomethane tests at Camp Lejeune and could not finish them. A note on a Hadnot Point sample form dated 30 October 1980 reads: "Water is highly contaminated with low molecular weight halogenated hydrocarbons." On samples dated 9 March 1981, on the form catalogued as CLW 0443, the Army's own laboratory wrote: "Water highly contaminated with other chlorinated hydrocarbons (solvents)!" A private laboratory reported the same thing in 1982. The contaminated Hadnot Point wells came out of service between November 1984 and February 1985; the Tarawa Terrace plant closed in 1987. The families were not told. Ensminger learned of the contamination in August 1997, by accident, as a civilian — and started filing Freedom of Information Act requests that filled a binder he has kept ever since.

The measured maxima in drinking water were 215 micrograms per liter of PCE at Tarawa Terrace and 1,400 of TCE at Hadnot Point, against a federal limit of five — a limit that did not exist until 1989 and 1992. This film states exactly what the record supports and no more: it does not prove anyone in 1981 understood what those chemicals do to a body, and a federal criminal investigation found no violation of federal law and was declined for prosecution in 2007. What it proves is narrower. The institution measured its own water, wrote down that the water was heavily contaminated, took years to turn off the taps, and then did not go and find the people who had been drinking it.

On the science, the language matters. ATSDR's 2017 review found sufficient evidence for causation between TCE and kidney cancer and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, PCE and bladder cancer, benzene and leukemias, and vinyl chloride and liver cancer — chemical to disease, never chemical to person. A 2024 cancer incidence study comparing Camp Lejeune personnel with Camp Pendleton concluded that "increased risks of several cancers were observed among Marines/Navy personnel and civilian workers exposed to contaminated drinking water at Camp Lejeune compared with Camp Pendleton." Whether the water caused any particular person's illness is a question no study has answered. There is also no official total for how many people were exposed; the figure of around a million comes from a congressional hearing in 2010, not from a health agency. Ensminger's own sworn words are "hundreds of thousands of Marines, sailors, their families, and the loyal civilian employees who were unknowingly exposed."

Mike Partain was conceived, carried and born at Camp Lejeune in 1968. He testified to Congress in 2010: "'You have male breast cancer' were the words which greeted me and my wife on our 18th wedding anniversary." He had located 63 other men with the same rare cancer and a connection to the same water; the count he keeps now runs past 125. That list is a registry one man assembled, not epidemiology — when federal researchers tested the question in 2015 with 71 cases against 373 controls, the odds ratio came out at 1.14 with a confidence interval running through 1. On 28 April 2009 ATSDR withdrew its own 1997 public health assessment of the base, because it had left out benzene.

For thirty years North Carolina's statute of repose kept these claims out of court, and about 4,000 of them were dismissed in December 2016. Congress answered with the Janey Ensminger Act, signed 6 August 2012, and then the Camp Lejeune Justice Act, section 804 of the PACT Act, signed 10 August 2022 — which waived immunity, took the statute of repose off the board, and set the burden at "sufficient to conclude that a causal relationship is at least as likely as not." Law firms spent nearly $112 million on television advertising for claimants in 2022 alone. The filing window closed, for almost everyone, on 10 August 2024.

As of the government's 15 June 2026 filing: 408,000 de-duplicated administrative claims, 3,759 lawsuits, roughly 2,446 people paid, $723,850,000 in total payments. Three of the twenty-five bellwether cases had settled — $10,000, $24,000, and $405. Not one case has been tried. On 30 June 2026 the court reappointed the plaintiffs' leadership group only until 30 October 2026, ordered weekly settlement meetings, and wrote that it expects both sides "to use their best efforts to achieve a global settlement by October 30, 2026." No court has ever ruled on whether the United States is liable, and no individual has ever been publicly disciplined or prosecuted over the contamination.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic, and no real-person likeness is shown.

Sources include: the sworn congressional testimony of Jerry Ensminger (2007) and Mike Partain (2010); the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry; United States Army Environmental Hygiene Agency laboratory records; Grainger Laboratories correspondence; Bove and colleagues in Environmental Health Perspectives and in Environmental Health; Ruckart and colleagues in Environmental Health; the Janey Ensminger Act; the Camp Lejeune Justice Act, section 804 of the PACT Act; orders and filings of the United States District Court for the Eastern District of North Carolina; and the United States Department of Justice.

#CampLejeune #ToxicExposure #Veterans #PACTAct #MarineCorps #PrimeDocumentary

robosigning.title: He Paid $139,000 Cash. There Was No Mortgage. The Bank Padlocked the Door.
robosigning.description:
On 9 January 2010, Charlie Cardoso stood outside a house in Spring Hill, Florida, and cut the padlocks off his own front door. He and his wife Maria had bought it in March 2005 for $139,000, in cash — the price and the year come from newspaper reporting citing county records, and the complaint calls it his life savings. There had never been a mortgage on it. No lender, no lien, no note, and a deed recorded at the county that anyone could have walked in and read.

In late June 2009 their tenant telephoned in a panic: three men from Bank of America were at the property to foreclose. The house was cleaned out and padlocked. The house the bank meant to take was across the street, about ten doors down. Bank of America's own listing agent contacted the bank to say it was foreclosing on the wrong home. On 5 January 2010 a representative told Cardoso the bank had made a mistake and that someone would call him back within the hour. Nobody ever called back. His son drove him 1,300 miles from Massachusetts. He bought a bolt cutter, cut every lock, and broke in through the back screen door. The pipes had frozen, the tools and the family photographs were gone, and only what was in the attic was still there. They filed suit in federal court on 20 January 2010.

To take a house through a court, a bank hands a judge a sworn affidavit — one named human being swearing, on penalty of perjury, that they have personal knowledge of the facts. Most homeowners in foreclosure have no lawyer, and in many cases the affidavit is the only evidence there is. On 10 December 2009, under oath, Jeffrey Stephan — a team leader in GMAC Mortgage's document execution unit, a mid-level employee whose own sworn testimony is the only basis on which this film describes him — said his team brought him "approximately, I'd say a round number of ten thousand" documents a month. Asked, "So these documents wouldn't be actually executed on your own personal knowledge?", he answered: "Right." In a second deposition in June 2010 he put it at 400 a day, said he did not read the paragraphs or inspect the exhibits, and confirmed he did not appear before the notary. Maine's highest court called the resulting filing "a disturbing example of a reprehensible practice."

It was done at industrial scale in an office park in Alpharetta, Georgia, by a company called DocX, owned by Lender Processing Services. According to the United States Department of Justice, from at least March 2003 until late 2009 DocX prepared and filed more than one million fraudulently signed and notarised mortgage documents with property recorders' offices across the country, on about $60 million of revenue. One name is on more of them than any other, and the woman it belongs to did nothing wrong: Linda Green was a real auto-parts shipping clerk who took a job at DocX in 2003, she has said she was never a bank vice president, and she was never charged with anything — DocX made her one because, she said, her name was short and easy to spell, and as demand grew other people wrote it, in a dozen different hands. One of them, Chris Pendley, was paid $10 an hour against a floor of 350 signatures an hour. A colleague at the next desk notarised what he signed. Every page went to a county recorder, which is where the country keeps the record of who owns what.

When a Bank of America official testified she had signed 7,000 to 8,000 foreclosure documents a month without reading them, the machine stopped very fast. GMAC halted evictions in 23 states on 20 September 2010; JPMorgan Chase suspended more than 50,000 foreclosures; Bank of America froze foreclosures in the same 23 states on 1 October and in all fifty on 8 October. Those 23 are the states where a judge has to be handed the paperwork — which is the only reason anyone ever looked at it. All fifty attorneys general opened a joint investigation on 13 October. Seventeen days after it stopped, it restarted: Bank of America said it would process affidavits in 102,000 proceedings, and Wells Fargo said it would file supplemental affidavits in 55,000 actions.

The reckoning was announced on 9 February 2012 at $25 billion. Of that, $1.5 billion — six percent — was cash to people whose homes had already been taken. Cheques went out in June 2013: 962,278 valid claims at about $1,480 each. The parallel remedy, the Independent Foreclosure Review, was supposed to open every 2009 and 2010 foreclosure file and find out who had actually been harmed; it was terminated on 7 January 2013 with final reviews completed on about 14 percent of the files and not one consultant having finished their sample, after regulators were told that finishing would cost at least $2 billion more in consultants' fees against roughly $1.2 billion of remediation. The replacement paid borrowers, in the Federal Reserve's own words, "regardless of whether the borrower had suffered financial injury caused by servicer error": 2,358,441 people out of the 3,949,896 in the Fed's published table received $300, while 1,082 received $125,000. There is no number, anywhere, for how many American foreclosures rested on manufactured documents, because the only mechanism ever built to count them was switched off. Exactly one person went to federal prison over any of it — Lorraine Brown, DocX's chief executive, who pleaded guilty on 20 November 2012 and was sentenced on 25 June 2013 to five years. Lender Processing Services signed a non-prosecution agreement and paid $35 million.

The paper is moving again. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has documented "zombie second mortgages" — loans most borrowers last paid in 2015 or earlier, sold to debt collectors and resurfacing as foreclosure threats — and in January 2025 found that one or more companies had failed to send those homeowners the statements the law requires. A class action in Massachusetts alleges a servicer and a trustee failed, as a matter of systematic internal policy, to send billing statements to borrowers whose second mortgages had been discharged in bankruptcy, and then moved to foreclose. Meanwhile, in the Government Accountability Office's own words, since February 2025 the Bureau has been reducing the size and scope of its activities and staffing: a funding cap halved by statute in July 2025, stop-work orders, closed examinations, terminated enforcement cases, and reduction-in-force notices covering the overwhelming majority of its staff — a plan a federal court has so far blocked, with the litigation still live as this film goes out.

Some imagery in this film is AI-assisted and symbolic, and no real-person likeness is shown.

Sources include: the amended complaints and docket in Cardoso v. Bank of America in the United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts; St. Petersburg Times reporting by Tony Marrero; the sworn depositions of Jeffrey Stephan of December 2009 and June 2010; Federal National Mortgage Association v. Bradbury in the Maine Supreme Judicial Court; the United States Department of Justice; the Florida Attorney General's economic crimes division presentation; CBS 60 Minutes; the Congressional Oversight Panel; the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; the Government Accountability Office; the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau; the Nevada Attorney General; the Missouri Attorney General; CoreLogic; and the Associated Press.

#RoboSigning #ForeclosureCrisis #MortgageFraud #HousingCrisis #ConsumerProtection #PrimeDocumentary

It rests on the sworn federal complaint (RS-04/RS-05) plus independent St. Petersburg Times reporting; the case settled in April 2011 with terms never made public and no court finding was ever made against the bank. The tag 'Linda Green signature' refers to the signature motif, not the woman - confirm it cannot read as an accusation.

Circuit limited remand 19 June 2026; RIF litigation stayed 10 July 2026; nominee hearing 23 July 2026; acting-director succession from 1 August 2026). The 88% RIF percentage is deliberately NOT used and must stay out unless re-verified against the GAO slides.

Never state or imply that robo-signing has not recurred (RS-88 is 'not found by this pass', not 'does not exist').
